definition: Predetermine means to decide or set something in advance, before it actually happens or before all the facts are in.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word predetermine. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know predetermine should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Critics accused the coach of trying to predetermine the starting lineup before tryouts had even begun.
Planning sketches what you intend to do but leaves room for change; predetermining locks in the outcome itself before events even play out.
Preordain is stronger than predetermine — it suggests an outcome fixed by fate or absolute authority that no one can alter.

Prearrange means to organize the practical details of something ahead of time — a prearranged meeting point, a prearranged signal. It covers logistics: where, when, how. Predetermine goes to the outcome itself: the result is decided before the process plays out. You prearrange the ceremony; critics accuse you of predetermining the verdict.

Preset means to fix a setting in advance, usually on a machine or system — a preset temperature, preset radio stations. It is mechanical and neutral. Predetermine is about outcomes and decisions, and often carries suspicion: a predetermined result suggests the open process was a sham. Dials are preset; verdicts are predetermined.

To rig something is to fix its result dishonestly — a rigged raffle has been manipulated so the fair-looking process is fake. Rigging is always cheating. Predetermine is broader and not always corrupt: a coach can openly predetermine a lineup. Every rigged contest is predetermined, but a predetermined outcome may involve no fraud at all.

For decades, popular psychology insisted that birth order shaped destiny: firstborns led, youngest children charmed, middle children negotiated.
The claim was that a single fact of family position could predetermine an adult's personality before school, friendships, or work had any say.
When researchers finally tracked thousands of siblings into adulthood, the pattern collapsed.
Position in the family predicted almost nothing once the data were sorted; experience, it turned out, kept rewriting whatever the cradle had begun.
The lesson was not that early life is powerless, but that no single early fact settles the outcome in advance.
